	At age 40, Taylor is set to go into boxing retirement no matter the outcome of the title bout. Win or lose, she would go down in history as one of the most iconic female boxer of all-time. However, if Taylor does end up with the undisputed title again (it would be her third time), it would be the end of an era and a storybook ending to an exceptional career in boxing. But, if Pili wins the bout, it would be like Taylor passing the torch to a new generation of fighter.

title: Al Pacino Sends Video Message to Venice After Missing Press Conference for ‘Father Joe’: ‘I Wish I Was There, I Really Do’
description: Al Pacino didn’t travel to the Venice Film Festival for the premiere of “Father Joe,” but he sent a video message with well wishes to his collaborat
body:
Al Pacino didn’t travel to the Venice Film Festival for the premiere of “Father Joe,” but he sent a video message with well wishes to his collaborators on the movie.

	“I wish I was there with all of you in Venice, which is great and lovely. I’ve had films there. I’ve been there. I’ve experienced it,” said a sunglass-clad Pacino before he shouted out writer-producer Luc Besson (“It’s great to say his name”) and his co-star Kiefer Sutherland. “Have a good one. Best to you all.”
	

	“Father Joe,” starring Sutherland, Pacino and Ever Anderson, takes place in 1990s Manhattan’s Little Italy and revolves around a priest who clashes with a mob boss. The action thriller was written and produced by Besson and marks the directing debut of Barthélémy Grossmann. Grossmann has referred to “Father Joe” as a “modern fable about faith, redemption and the complexity of human nature.”


	Sutherland plays the titular Father Joe, described as “a man of God unlike any other” who wages a secret war — singlehandedly busting crime rings and turning the city’s underworld into his congregation. Pacino plays a powerful crime lord whose empire collides with Father Joe’s crusade. Anderson portrays a young woman caught between danger and redemption under Joe’s guidance. 

	Sutherland said he was drawn to the project — which he called a meditation on “good vs. evil” — because of Besson’s involvement.

	“I was a huge, huge fan,” Sutherland said. “Luc had made films I wish I had been in. I thought, ‘That is the kind of movie I should be making.’ But he never hired me. Very fortunately, he thought of me for this idea.”
	

	Besson is the influential French director of “The Fifth Element,” “Lucy” and most recently, a “Dracula” remake starring Caleb Landry Jones and Christoph Waltz. He one of the first prominent figures in France to face sexual assault allegations in the #MeToo era. He was accused of rape by Belgian-Dutch female actor Sand Van Roy, though Besson was eventually cleared of all charges.

	Besson described a hands-off style as a producer on “Father Joe.”

	“The good thing is I’m also a director. I don’t want to be bothered when I’m a director so I tried not to bother,” Besson said. “I’m on the back of Barthélémy. As long as he doesn’t have a problem, I’m not there.”

schema.headline: Al Pacino Sends Video Message to Venice After Missing Press Conference for ‘Father Joe’: ‘I Wish I Was There, I Really Do’

title: Louis Garrel Jokes About ‘Moretti Method’ Acting at Press Conference for Nanni Moretti’s ‘It Will Happen Tonight’
description: Veteran auteur Nanni Moretti – who has had nine movies in competition at Cannes — is back in Venice after 37 years with “It Will Happen Tonight,” a
body:
Veteran auteur Nanni Moretti – who has had nine movies in competition at Cannes — is back in Venice after 37 years with “It Will Happen Tonight,” a romantic drama toplining French star Louis Garrel and Italian A-lister Jasmine Trinca (“La Storia,” “Supersex”).

	“Years ago I had coined this slightly stupid phrase that I used to say at press conferences: ‘I want to keep making the same film; but possibly make it more beautiful each time,'” Moretti said, after being greeted warmly at the film’s presser. Then, as time progressed, the director said he decided he wanted to try new things. This time, with his screenwriters, Valia Santella and Federica Pontremoli, “we imagined a pretty powerful love story,” Moretti said.
	

	Romance, in terms of genre, is a first for the idiosyncratic director who has often constructed his films around his own persona, appearing as the central character. Starting with his 1976 Super-8 debut “Io Sono un’Autarchico” and its follow-up, “Ecce Bombo,” which humorously captured the discontent gripping Italy in the bleak 1970s, and, of course, the autobiografical “Caro Diario,” 1994, which marked his international breakthrough. Moretti subsequent standout works comprise his 2001 Palm d’Or winning bereavement drama “The Son’s Room,” the scathing 2006 Silvio Berlusconi satire “The Caiman” and “We Have a Pope” in which he depicted a Pontiff’s crisis of faith.


	“It Will Happen Tonight” is loosely based on the short story collection “Hungry Heart” (Lev Raev) by Israeli writer Eshkol Nevo. Moretti, in his director’s statement, called them “Stories about love, encounters and partings. But also about parents and their grown-up children. And all those bonds that accompany us – more or less quietly – throughout our lives.” 
	

	The film reunites Moretti with Trinca who made her acting debut in “The Son’s Room” in 2001, when Trinca was 18, and subsequently appeared in the “The Caiman.” 

	“It’s been hugely emotional to be back working with him,” said Trinca, who was on the Cannes jury in 2023. “Nanni is the person who forged my idea of cinema. Which is not about being in front of camera with an affectation or a pose.”

	“It Will Happen Tonight” instead marks Moretti’s first collaboration with Garrel, who starred in French blockbusters “The Three Musketeers” parts 1 and 2 and will soon be seen alongside Sydney Sweeney in Studiocanal’s “Custom of the Country.”

	Garrel humorously recounted what he called “the Moretti [acting] method.” For a scene in which the actor had to play basketball, Garrel arrived on set and found the director on the court. Moretti picked up the ball, shot a perfect hoop on his first shot, as cameras were rolling, and told Garrel: “This is what I want you to do,” the actor recounted. “Twenty-five takes later – when I had failed to put the ball through the basket – he sadistically told the crew: “Can I see the shot I took?”

	The film’s cast also comprises Angela Finocchiaro, Elena Lietti, Antonio De Matteo, Andrea Lattanzi, Hippolyte Girardot, Pietro Ragusa, and Paolo Sassanelli.

	Moretti most recently competed in Cannes in 2023 with high-concept meta-comedy “A Brighter Tomorrow,” in which he stars as a Roman director who is shooting a period piece set in Rome in 1956.

	Sacher Film and Fandango produced “It Will Happen Tonight” in collaboration with RAI Cinema.

	Paris-based Playtime and French distributor and producer Pan-Européenne, which are handling sales, have presold “It Will Happen Tonight” widely ahead of its festival bow.

schema.headline: Louis Garrel Jokes About ‘Moretti Method’ Acting at Press Conference for Nanni Moretti’s ‘It Will Happen Tonight’

title: ‘Our Share of Sand’ Review: A Brooding Indian Social Drama Told Through the Eyes of a Young Girl
description: A keenly observed class drama shown through the eyes of a child, Shalini Adnani’s “” overcomes its characters’ narrow construction through its brood
body:
A keenly observed class drama shown through the eyes of a child, Shalini Adnani’s “” overcomes its characters’ narrow construction through its brooding intensity. Set against a sand-mining crisis in modern India, it tells of a 12-year-old British Asian girl, Maya (Maya Mehta), who returns to the country to join her industrialist father Rohan (Mohammad Zeeshan Ayyub), and bears witness to a routine accident in his line of work. As notions of justice, power and inequity begin to shade her peripheral vision, Maya is torn between speaking out and adhering to the moral compartmentalization that goes hand in hand with her family’s generational success.
	

	Adnani, a Chilean-born Londoner of Indian descent, draws on her memories of visiting India as a young outsider in crafting the film’s atmosphere, and her protagonist’s confined perspective. Such an approach runs the risk of gawking at an unfamiliar people, their hegemonies and their ways of life, even with the best intentions. But by rooting her tale in Maya’s family ties, the writer-director explores the complicity of well-to-do South Asian diasporas, and the foundations that afford them the luxury of emigrating in the first place. It begins with a brief, poetic prologue set decades ago — seemingly outside of time — as obscured day-laborers sift through sandy riverbanks and discover an enormous diamond. Their faces remain hidden, as a debate ensues about whether they should alert their boss to its discovery.


	The next time we see this diamond, in a contemporary setting, Maya’s stern paternal aunt, Arti (Jyoti Dogra), shows it off while regaling her with their family’s mythology, wherein her grandfather discovered the gem and sold a fragment of it to uplift them after postcolonial partition. It’s worth noting that the aforementioned quandary, about alerting the laborers’ boss, is never answered: Did the grandfather really find the diamond himself, as a worker, or did he simply claim it from his employees?
	

	There’s no way to prove the veracity of this “bootstraps” creation myth, a lingering doubt that informs the film’s saga of cyclical inequality. This initially takes unassuming form, as Maya grows friendly with Kiran (Krish Raj More), a boy of a similar age. There’s already a division between them — Maya doesn’t speak much Hindi or Marathi (the local language), while Kiran doesn’t speak English, though they just about understand each other — which is only reinforced when Maya’s father scolds Kiran to get back to work.

	The adolescent turning out to be in Rohan’s employ ought to come as no surprise: Caste and class remain inflexible facets of Indian society, including on the outskirts of Mumbai, where the film is set. Kiran, dismissively treated, is one of Rohan’s divers, and a vital manual laborer in the cement production chain laying the foundation for India’s modern development. It isn’t long before Rohan’s regulation-skirting methods leads to an accident by nightfall, which leaves Kiran permanently injured. This in turn leads Maya (a key witness) and her British Indian mother Priti (Ellora Torchia) to quietly question what they ought to say to the police — if anything at all.  

	Although the film never gives its divisions a name — much of it unfolds through Maya’s sheltered perspective — its setting provides the perfect symbolism for a nation built on discrimination. Caste becomes a silent killer, as the expectations foisted upon Rohan’s workers collide with subdued pleas for their humanity. (Some of them are understandably furious, but others know there’s only so much they can say.) Granted, most characters barely exist outside the confines of the plot, and how they relate to social strata is their defining characteristic. We know little about Maya’s life before her arrival, or Kiran’s outside his work, or the family beyond their casual cruelty. But within this storytelling paradigm, Adnani imbues each scene with a dramatic wrath bubbling just beneath the surface.

	This tension is often subtext enough, and it’s accentuated by cinematographer Adric Watson’s tight and dirty frames, which confine Maya and Arti through astute visual composition, as the reality of their cushy lives is gradually illuminated. There’s also occasional use of night photography, by way of the family compound’s security cameras where you wouldn’t expect them, gesturing at a thematic handshake between the upkeep of caste superiority and fascistic surveillance. It’s the closest “Our Share of Sand” gets to casting a wide net over India’s contemporary political milieu, and while this facet remains largely unexplored, the film’s confining focus on Maya’s point of view pays a number of dramatic dividends.
	

	Not only does Mehta deliver a stunning debut performance, as a young girl perturbed by the world and her place within it, but the film’s sinister, shadowy tone makes even natural spaces feel imposing. The result is a twisted, naturalistic fairytale about structural realities; with the right boot-heel at one’s neck, even ostensibly life-giving forces like forests and rivers can be turned against innocent people.

schema.headline: ‘Our Share of Sand’ Review: A Brooding Indian Social Drama Told Through the Eyes of a Young Girl

title: Liam and Noel Gallagher Skip Oasis Documentary Press Conference at Venice Film Festival
description: In news that might not surprise anyone, Liam and Noel Gallagher skipped the Venice Film Festival press conference for their upcoming Disney+ documen
body:
In news that might not surprise anyone, Liam and Noel Gallagher skipped the Venice Film Festival press conference for their upcoming Disney+ documentary “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger” on Saturday.

	The two brothers — who reunited last year for their massive “Live ’25” tour after a 15-year feud — arrived on the Lido in a boat, took photos for the film’s photocall and then left before the conference. Present at the presser were co-directors Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace as well as Steven Knight, who is credited as the creator of the doc.
	

	Asked during the presser why the Gallaghers weren’t on hand, Lovelace said: “They were here a second ago having their photograph taken, so they are here,” but did not elaborate further. The brothers were apparently never scheduled to appear at the conference, though journalists and fans in the room seemed to not be aware of this.


	Variety has reached out to representatives for Oasis and Disney for comment.

	Liam and Noel have been press shy as a pair since their reunion, only sitting for an interview together for “Don’t Look Back in Anger” — their first in 20 years. The documentary, which is world premiering at Venice on Saturday night, releases in theaters Sept. 11 before bowing on Disney+ later this year, boasts footage of the band both backstage and onstage.

	The brothers also may have wanted to dodge questions regarding rumors about a new tour, with the band posting cryptic teasers on social media the past two days. Noel Gallagher also nodded to a potential 2027 tour in an interview with Talksport recently, saying: “Let’s put it this way: there’s no football tournament on next year, so we’ve got to do something in the summer, right?”
	

	In an interview with Variety, Southern and Lovelace broke down how they went about capturing the Liam and Noel’s reunion, including setting up hidden cameras in their rehearsal space. 

	“We didn’t want it to feel mediated. We didn’t want it to feel like there’s an annoying camera crew running around getting in their way,” Southern said. “And we were aware of how sensitive it was, and that this was literally the first time they’d been in a room together for a prolonged period for 15 years.”

	However, don’t expect the Gallagher Brothers to get all mushy in the documentary. “It’s the Gallaghers, it’s not ‘Dawson’s Creek,'” Southern added. “They’re not gonna sit down and talk about their emotions.”

schema.headline: Liam and Noel Gallagher Skip Oasis Documentary Press Conference at Venice Film Festival

title: Aflac Taps Affleck for Commercials to Keep Insurance Customers Quacking
description: It seems as simple as moving a few letters around, but a new collaboration between Aflac, the provider of supplemental insurance and Ben Affleck, th
body:
It seems as simple as moving a few letters around, but a new collaboration between Aflac, the provider of supplemental insurance and Ben Affleck, the actor and director, has been years in the making.

	Pairing Aflac, which has thrived with commercials featuring an anthropomorphic duck squawking out its name, and Affleck. the star of “Good Will Hunting,” “Gone Girl” and “Argo,” is an idea that has been in the ether for some time, acknowledges Garth Knutson, the insurer’s senior vice president and chief marketing officer. “This has probably been tens of thousands of peoples’ idea,” he says during a recent interview. “It’s one of those things that people just make as a joke. Even Ben has been joking about it for a long time — maybe he has been a little bit more annoyed in the past.”
	

	Aflac has struck a partnership with Artists Equity, the production studio founded by Affleck, Matt Damon and financier Gerry Cardinale, and their first new work shows up Saturday during ESPN’s “College GameDay,” and, subsequently, in other types of sports programming, including ESPN’s “Monday Night Football,” and in connected-TV inventory. In the first new ad, Affleck gets a lesson from popular coaches Nick Saban, Deion “Coach Prime” Sanders and Dawn Staley on what Aflac does and how supplemental coverage can help consumers.


	The star power shines a light on the increasingly competitive nature of advertising from top insurance companies. Aflac initially gained a bigger profile after introducing its duck mascot in 1999, in ads crafted by Kaplan Thaler Group, an independent agency that was eventually acquired by Publicis Groupe of France. The duck flew on to Madison Avenue just months after the debut of the Geico Gecko, another popular insurance mascot.
	

	In the intervening decades, the average consumer has likely encountered Jake From State Farm; Progressive’s Flo and her colleagues Jamie and Mara, not to mention Dr. Rick; Allstate’s Mayhem; Geico’s Cavemen; and Farmers Insurance’s Professor Burke. Liberty Mutual recently expanded its gallery of characters with a fuzzy yellow creature called Liberty Biberty. The challenge for Aflac is that many of the aforementioned insurance companies spend $1 billion or more annually on advertising, with Progressive spending more than $4 billion, according to data from S&P Global and Dowling & Partners. 

	Aflac typically spends under $100 million on U.S. advertising, according to MediaRadar, a tracker of ad spending. Keep in mind: Aflac is more of a specialist, selling supplemental insurance that pays out extra cash benefits for out-of-pocket costs and bills that are not covered by primary health insurance.

	Does Knutson feel he’s under pressure to stand out? “I think about it all the time,” he says. “The answer is, ‘Absolutely, yes.'”

	He has a few tools within easy reach. The Duck, he says, “is extremely cheap for a celebrity, at least from a payment standpoint. He works for bread, a different kind of bread than what you or I work for.” He also has the support of the company’s senior executives. Aflac CEO Daniel Amos has run the company for decades and played a role in launching the waterfowl into advertising stardom.

	Still, says Knutson, “we have to punch above our weight.” Consumers might not encounter Aflac ads in as many places as they do commercials from others, he says, but the company hopes “that people who do see them are more inclined to remember the message and, hopefully, act on it.” 

	Artists Equity has made a name for itself as a producer of commercials that command attention. Among its best-known efforts are a series of Super Bowl ads from Dunkin that feature Affleck and several famous associates, and a spot for Stella Artois that pairs Damon with soccer great David Beckham.

	Affleck was extremely involved in the process, says Knutson. “If we had twelve creative reviews with them, Ben was in all of the first six of them,” he recalls. In many cases, a celebrity featured in a commercial doesn’t start working on it until much later in the process, he notes. Indeed, an agency might tap a young associate to read lines that a star will handle for the finished product. “That speaks to how intertwined he and his team have been in this project.”
	

	New Aflac/Affleck ads are expected to run into 2027, says the executive. A second flight will begin to surface around Thanksgiving, around the time many employees are considering insurance options during open-enrollment processes. And in March, Aflac will have a presence alongside some notable entertainment properties, says Knutson, without offering further detail.

	The initial contact between Aflac and Affleck came after Knutson talked about the concept with his boss, Virgil Miller, president of the insurance company. From there, Knutson sent a “cold email” to the Artists Equity executive he thought would be most appropriate. When the two companies met to discuss concepts, Knutson was surprised by how much of Affleck’s interest his team had captured. “To have an agency founder who also happens to be a celebrity asking smart questions about supplemental health insurance? It really blew me over.”

schema.headline: Aflac Taps Affleck for Commercials to Keep Insurance Customers Quacking

title: Marion Cotillard Praises Venice Biennale College Cinema Workshop: ‘Not all Films Are Destined to Draw Millions of Viewers and Turn a Profit’
description: Oscar-winner Marion Cotillard (“La Vie en Rose”) is at the Venice Film Festival in a new guise, as tutor of Biennale College Cinema, the workshop al
body:
Oscar-winner Marion Cotillard (“La Vie en Rose”) is at the Venice Film Festival in a new guise, as tutor of Biennale College Cinema, the workshop allowing emerging filmmakers to develop and produce micro-budget feature-length films, which is sponsored by Chanel.

	Biennale College Cinemas was conceived 15 years ago by Venice chief Alberto Barbera in tandem with Torino Film Lab topper Savina Neirotti, who heads the unique Venice initiative. 
	

	During this time Biennale College has spawned 49 feature film projects made with micro-budgets with grants that after the first decade rose from €150,00 ($174,00) to €200,00 ($232) during the past five years. “These works provide a bird’s eye view of what it means to debut as a filmmaker today,” Neirotti noted.


	“When Chanel told me about this program, I was very touched,” said Cotillard. “Above all, I think it’s very important to support films that are struggling to get off the ground financially these days,” she added.

	“Not all films are destined to draw millions of viewers and turn a profit, and I think it’s very important to support artists — artists from all over the world – some of whom, even in their own countries, simply don’t have access to production opportunities,” she noted. 

	“And what’s really striking about the films I’ve seen — the four films I’ve seen – is their artistic passion; that need to tell stories,” Cotillard continued. 

	This year’s Biennale College projects, all first works, hail from China, Italy, Mexico, Spain and the U.S. They are: “Demeter in Exile,” by Italian director Maria Giovanna Cicciari, who is teamed with producer Raffaella Pontarelli; “Gu Shi,“ by Chinese director Yinan Song and produced by Yueyi Xing; “Moonfish,” by U.S. director Daniel Zvereff who is teamed with Spanish producer Mireia Villanova; and “Tijuana Todavía” by Mexian director Gabriel Gutierrez Morales working with producer Humberto Busto Marín.
	

	Barbera also said he will soon be announcing the winner of the first edition of Biennale College Blend, the initiative’s new strand for artists looking to explore stories in the multi-media space comprising forms of expression such as music, visual arts, and performing arts.

schema.headline: Marion Cotillard Praises Venice Biennale College Cinema Workshop: ‘Not all Films Are Destined to Draw Millions of Viewers and Turn a Profit’

title: ‘Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?’ Review: An Assaultive Yet Turgid and Outdated Vietnam PTSD Drama
description: If Shinya Tsukamoto‘s “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” were the first, or even the 51st, movie to litigate the atrocities committed by U.S. troops
body:
If Shinya Tsukamoto‘s “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” were the first, or even the 51st, movie to litigate the atrocities committed by U.S. troops during the Vietnam War, perhaps on a purely informational level some justification would exist for its crudely simplistic approach. Nuance is often a casualty of war, especially when that war is ongoing or recently ended. But this is 2026, when — in contrast to the era in which the real, evidently heroic Allen Nelson, on whose memoir the film is based, toured his cautionary horror story internationally — you’d be hard pressed to find a substantial contingent unaware that the Vietnam War has since been judged a mistake so costly in human life and dignity that it forced arguably the most substantial reevaluation of American self-identity since independence.
	

	Even still, reliving the dehumanizing cruelty of conflict and working through its aftermath might be a valuable exercise if new insights, uncovered through this one man’s PTSD journey, could then be scaled up and applied to the national psyche. And revisiting Vietnam through the eyes of a Black American, via the outsider perspective of the Japanese director of “Tetsuo: The Iron Man,” no less, must surely deliver some new insights? But despite half taking place in a therapist’s office, “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” is only invested in its lead’s psychology insofar as it provides the excuse for a series of increasingly grisly and violent flashbacks, and has nothing but the most cursory and stereotype-laden interest in the effect of the war on the African-American community specifically.
	

	Marine Allen Nelson (played by Mark Merphy as a younger man and Rodney Hicks as his older counterpart) has recently returned from the front in severe shellshock. Unwilling to subject his family to his bouts of paranoia and rage, he is dossing in a filthy, boarded-up building in New York City, with only a straggly cat and the fat, oily alley rats for company. Furtively darting out to shoplift some supplies one day, he is accosted by an old classmate who brightly announces she is now a schoolteacher and invites him to speak about his war experiences to her class. He demurs initially. 

	But then, some boys throw bangers nearby, and he finds himself diving for cover under a nearby car, where, in one of the film’s more effectively abstract evocations of a dissociative episode, he watches the slice of pavement visible from his vantage point reverberating to the deafening chaos of explosions and gunfire in his mind. He shows up at the class, lathered in sweat (the sweat-spray and gunshot-squib cost for this film must represent a sizeable portion of its budget) and hesitantly begins to speak. But he is unable to answer the moppet who — in a sentimental, heavily-leaned-into close-up — poses the question that gave Nelson’s original memoir, and gives Tsukamoto’s film, its name.

	Years later, Nelson is married to Linda (pity poor Tatyana Ali, saddled with an almost comically underwritten, saintly-supportive-partner role) and is raising her son as his own. But he cannot sleep without medication to suppress his violent nightmares. After a particularly troubling outburst, he goes into therapy and, piece by piece, tells his story to Dr Daniels (Geoffrey Rush). These flashbacks betray where writer-director-cinematographer-editor Tsukamoto’s filmmaking interests really lie, which is in the gruesome recreation of hideous acts of barbarism and cruelty. Some of those, for good measure, he cuts into a montage, alongside rats gnawing on maggoty flesh and piles of moldering corpses, to deploy whenever things get boring back in one of the brown rooms of Allen’s present life. So, quite often.

	It is deeply unsavory that a film with such a ploddingly earnest anti-war message only comes alive in the depiction of violent, brutal death. As if aware of that, Tsukamoto seems to arrange the non-combat scenes as a penance, as though we, like the protagonist, must atone for the base thrills of warfare with endless tedious talk sessions. Hicks is a Broadway actor of some standing, but it’s very hard to tell here given that the ESL-style screenplay leaves him no register to work in other than sweatily anguished or, occasionally, sweatily relieved and illuminated in one of the rare shafts of sunlight allowed to penetrate Tsukamoto’s penumbral images.
	

	Rush, bringing what gravitas he can to a role that is essentially a dark brown sweater with eyes, compensates for essentially only having one line of dialogue (“Why did you kill people, Allen?”) by repeating it approximately one million times with slight variations of emphasis and formulation, until it finally elicits the breakthrough Allen needs. Beware this false dawn, however. It may have taken an eternity to get to, but this is only the first of many natural cutoff points where Tsukamoto could have put us out of our and Allen’s misery, only to instead fade up into yet another epilogue. 

	The film has maybe eight or ten endings — forgive the inexactness, you too may lose track of the number of times you are halfway out of your seat with one arm in the sleeve of your coat, before realizing that no, that very obvious dramatic beat was not the final bow, because now, suddenly Allen has a beard and a daughter! Oh, now his beard is gray. Oh, now he’s on a boat! And here is Lily Franky, the great Japanese actor who is fourth-billed but arrives at the eleventh hour to deliver a single monologue to a closed bathroom door. It is rare to come across a film — especially in a major festival’s competition lineup — in which not only does so little work, it is given such endless acreage in which to keep not working, which is especially striking given that there’s little in “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” that can’t be boiled down to: “Yes, I did.”

schema.headline: ‘Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?’ Review: An Assaultive Yet Turgid and Outdated Vietnam PTSD Drama

title: Robert Pattinson Wants Chris Hansen to Like ‘Primetime’ Despite His Criticisms: ‘I Hope the Inspiration His Character Has Given Is Some Kind of Compliment’
description: Robert Pattinson thinks Chris Hansen could come around on “Primetime,” a tense thriller about the television journalist and “To Catch a Predator” ho
body:
Robert Pattinson thinks Chris Hansen could come around on “Primetime,” a tense thriller about the television journalist and “To Catch a Predator” host, which premieres on Saturday afternoon at the Venice Film Festival. 

	The real-life Hansen has been vocal in his skepticism of the movie, which he said he hasn’t seen because he declined to sign a standard NDA from the studio, A24. But Hansen said that based on the trailer, he finds Pattinson’s portrayal “overly dramatic” and questioned Hollywood’s motives in dramatizing the popular Dateline NBC series about child predators. (However, Hansen admitted that his family “seem to think it’s a pretty good imitation.”)
	

	“Obviously, I hope he likes the movie,” Pattinson said on Saturday’s Venice Film Festival press conference. “There’s something electrifying about him. I would hope the amount of inspiration his character has given a lot of people for years is some kind of compliment.”


	Directed by Lance Oppenheim in his narrative feature debut, “Primetime” is set in the mid-2000s and follows Hansen, then the host of Dateline NBC’s “To Catch a Predator,” as he turns the pursuit of suspected child predators into primetime entertainment. Loosely based on the 2007 “Esquire” article “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die,” the movie exposes the ethical limits of Hansen’s methods and the collision between journalism, policing and entertainment. “To Catch a Predator” ultimately ended in 2008 after facing some backlash over its methods of confronting the suspects.

	“There’s something magnetic about his presence. I watched the show when I was younger and didn’t think about it,” Pattinson said. “There’s a strange alchemy — something he’s doing is the reason people are still talking about that show 20 years later. It’s not to do solely with the subject matter. It was something about the show that was groundbreaking, but then he’s someone centering it. There’s something, even after watching literally thousands of hours of it, you can’t put your finger on it.”
	

	Pattinson was joined at Saturday’s press conference by Oppenheim and co-stars Skyler Gisondo, Merritt Wever and Phoebe Bridgers. Pattinson praised Bridgers, the Grammy-winning singer and songwriter who makes her acting debut as a decoy in “Primetime.”

	“She’s unbelievable,” Pattinson said. “I didn’t even know Lance and Phoebe were friends. When he suggested her, I was like ‘Phoebe Bridgers? Why don’t we just get the queen?’ Even on the first day, she was so relaxed. She didn’t seem nervous at all. She completely got the tone, and it’s a relatively difficult movie.”

	Bridgers, for her part, described the filming process as “super intimidating.”

	“When Lance asked me, I was like, ‘No way, dude,'” she recalled. “But it turns out, working with incredible people actually makes it way easier. I thought I was going to wither with all of these guys. Instead, it was just fun and free.”

	Oppenheim, 30, is best known for documentaries like “Some Kind of Heaven,” “Spermworld” and the HBO series “Ren Faire.” He’s described “Primetime” as a “docu-fantasia,” a blend of his cinematic background. He remembers discovering “To Catch a Predator,” not through the show itself but through parodies on “South Park” and comedy website ebaum’s World. 

	“When I finally saw ‘To Catch a Predator,’ I was amazed,” Oppenheim said. “Chris Hansen had these one-liners like Tony Montana. But instead of ‘Say hello to my little friend,’ it was ”You see how this looks, right?’ I was always fascinated by the theatricality of the show. What happens when you turn one of the darkest subjects known to humankind into entertainment?”

	Pattinson is having quite a year, starring in box office hits like “The Drama” and Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster “The Odyssey” as well as Denis Villeneuve’s upcoming “Dune: Part III.” And his schedule isn’t mellowing any time soon: Pattinson traveled to Venice from London, where he’s filming “The Batman: Part II.”

	For what it’s worth, Pattinson doesn’t seem fazed by the nonstop clip of his work. “When you get the momentum going, it’s strangely not that hard,” Pattinson said. Plus, he cracked, “I just had a baby. I had no desire to go out at night, so suddenly I had twice as much time, which was helpful.”

	But he joked that after filming projects back-to-back-to-back, he noticed his characters blending together. 
	

	“I can definitely hear a little Chris Hansen in ‘The Odyssey’ when I watch it,” he said with a laugh. “It was literally hours apart!”

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson Wants Chris Hansen to Like ‘Primetime’ Despite His Criticisms: ‘I Hope the Inspiration His Character Has Given Is Some Kind of Compliment’

title: ‘Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass’ Review: The Famous Cat-and-Mouse Duo Are Not Themselves In a Chaotic Chinese Cartoon
description: That title gives a first clue towards how misbegotten and compromised this new Tom and Jerry joint is. Everybody knows that Tom and Jerry shouldn’t
body: That title gives a first clue towards how misbegotten and compromised this new Tom and Jerry joint is. Everybody knows that Tom and Jerry shouldn’t be searching for a forbidden compass, whatever that might be: If the perma-warring pair are on a quest for something, it ought to be, say, some pickles for a big cheese sandwich. The Hanna-Barbera cat and mouse — formerly a throwaway bunch of cartoons, now a ‘franchise’ — are all about triflingly menial disputes taken to absurd heights, leading to surreal sight gags and baroque violence.“Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass” gives us the most cursory of tributes to that mode in the film’s opening five minutes, as Jerry heads to a grand exhibition in New York called “Traveling Exhibition of the Astral Compass – Journey to the Enigmatic East.” (Edward Said fans are advised to bring bingo cards.) Tom is a security guard here, and forbids entrance to the little mouse, leading to a brief spate of chasing around the museum. This hubbub somehow awakens the mysterious powers of the titular compass, transporting the twosome to ‘Golden City’ in China, modeled after the Forbidden City, where a storyline based on Chinese mythology is about to get going. That is where all classic Tom and Jerry tomfoolery ends — and there are another 95 minutes to go.In Golden City we meet a character called Phoenix Master and his irritating sidekick Feeny, who resembles a thicc Big Bird with green hair coiffed à la Liberace. They have been sent down from heaven by the Celestial Master and must therefore find the compass again, with the aid of some anthropomorphic traditional roof decorations, such as ‘Sonny’, a green and pink icon of a god, or ‘Xander’, a horse-like creature. But in order to get the compass, they will have to defeat ‘Mega-Rat’, the movie’s villain, who labours away in a cave with his evil henchrats.That précis will give some idea of the alarming mental disconnect that the film puts viewers through, as it tosses Tom and indeed Jerry into this incomprehensible plot, in which the title characters will soon be reduced to the status of glorified onlookers. But before that, there’s time for a smattering of creaky scenes in which the Chinese characters mistake the American interlopers for deities and give them a sponsored-by-the-Tourism-Board visit of the premises. (“Ah, Golden Lake — when the spring flowers bloom, people come from all over! Isn’t it a beautiful sight?”) Some viewers may at this point be put in mind of “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom” — another tick on your Orientalism card, if you’re playing.The Chinese characters are animated in standard-issue knock-off Pixar mode, and therefore match up just about with Tom and Jerry 2.0, but the visuals around them are ceaselessly incoherent, adding to the already harrowing levels of chaos. Chinese traditional landscape painting commingles with manga-like warfare and knockabout gags Hollywood-style, and in the background of all the migraine-inducingly hyperactive shenanigans, there appear some upsettingly undifferentiated crowds of AI-faced villagers saying ‘rhubarb rhubarb’ to one another.Throughout, Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass feels bafflingly out of touch and off-key, with the flavor of supermarket own-brand cornflakes. To wit, a montage in which Tom and Jerry eat a buffet of noodles and dumplings while someone or other raps, “Tom and Jerry, you and I/We’re gonna make a million, gonna touch the sky” may have the paradoxical effect of making children clamor for some soothingly 2D cartoons from the 1940s.The film’s casual use of deeply American IP in order to sell what is unmistakably a Chinese property — produced by the state-owned China Film Group in partnership with Warner Bros. and Origin Animation — may be of interest to future students of geopolitics, but even as a spectacle for kids weaned on flashing lights and brainrot it is likely to be too jumbled and bewildering. As for the parent demographic, it will only appeal to that rare subset who actively dislike their children.

title: Lindsay Clancy Trial: Illinois Mom Allegedly Killed 2-Year-Old Son Hours After Texting About Case

                          Illinois Mom Allegedly Killed 2-Year-Old Son
body:
Lindsay Clancy Trial
                          Illinois Mom Allegedly Killed 2-Year-Old Son
                          After Texting About Case
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                September 4, 2026
                
                            3:45 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 4, 2026
                                4:44 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            An Illinois mother is accused of murdering her 2-year-old son hours after texting friends about the Lindsay Clancy trial.
      
    
            38-year-old Corie Walsh was initially hospitalized but then moved to a jail.
      
    
            Corie was arrested after cops came to her home on Tuesday. Officers arrived to find a 17-year-old neighbor giving the young child CPR. Law enforcement rushed the toddler to the hospital, where officials said he died.
      

            The neighbor said he found Corie in a room of the home harming herself. The incident came hours after Corie was chatting it up in a group text about the Lindsay Clancy murder case. 
      
    
            Prosecutors claim Corie told them she murdered her son because he was the devil. The police found a second young kid in the home, but he was unharmed. The two children’s father was not present. 
      
    
            The Will County Coroner’s Office ruled the child died by homicide. The cause of death has yet to be determined.

title: 2-Year-Old Girl Falls From Jersey Shore Amusement Park Ride
description:
Jersey Shore
                          Frightening Toddler Fall Shuts Down Ride
body:
Jersey Shore
                          Frightening Toddler Fall Shuts Down Ride
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 5, 2026
                            6:35 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            A 2-year-old girl fell from a chairlift-style amusement park ride on the Jersey Shore.
      
    
            The toddler was riding Casino Pier's Sky Ride in Seaside Heights, NJ, with her aunt and a 3-year-old boy Monday night when she tumbled from the chair before the ride began moving.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The girl reportedly fell onto the edge of the boardwalk's entrance platform before landing in the sand below ... a drop of roughly 10 to 12 feet.
      

            The ride was quickly shut down, leaving the 3-year-old boy stranded in his chair. Firefighters later used a ladder to safely bring him back down.
      
    
            EMS staff checked out the toddler before she and her aunt were taken to Community Medical Center in Toms River for evaluation.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Police say the ride appeared to be functioning properly, with no obvious defects or signs of a malfunction.
      
    
            The New Jersey Department of Community Affairs is investigating.

title: 'Wheel of Fortune' Fires Jim Thornton After Pedophile Chatroom Incident
description:
Jim Thornton
                          'Wheel of Fortune' Fires Him After Pedo Chat Incident
body:
Jim Thornton
                          'Wheel of Fortune' Fires Him After Pedo Chat Incident
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                September 4, 2026
                
                            1:51 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 4, 2026
                                4:39 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jim Thornton is 86'd from "Wheel of Fortune" ... TMZ has learned Sony Pictures Television Studios dropped the hammer Friday afternoon.
      
    
            A Sony spokesperson tells us ... "Following a thorough investigation, Jim Thornton’s employment with Wheel of Fortune has been terminated, effective immediately."
      
    
            The firing comes days after TMZ broke the story ... Thornton was flying American Airlines to Los Angeles in May when a passenger spotted him on what she believed to be a chatroom for pedophiles.
      

            You can see in the photos ... disturbing messages mentioned "couple of cute boys and a hot little girl," as well as "All-you-can-eat Boyfett."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            There were also several references to "CP" ... often online shorthand for child porn.
      
    
            Although Thornton has not been charged with a crime, the producers of 'Wheel' moved quickly after conducting their own investigation. Sources with direct knowledge tell us an interim announcer will be heard when the new season begins on September 14, and Thornton's been removed from the show's social channels.
      
    
            As we previously reported, a passenger on that American Airlines flight spotted his screen, notified a flight attendant who alerted the pilot ... who ultimately contacted authorities.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Law enforcement met the plane when it landed at LAX -- the authorities questioned Thornton about the incident, but he was ultimately free to leave.
      
    
            Jim's lawyer previously told TMZ the whole thing was seemingly a big mix-up -- she says Jim often visited a suicide prevention chat forum, chat.988lifeline.org, to help people struggling with suicidal ideation.
      
    
            But Jim claims he had been sent the wrong link and wound up on lifeline.chat, which is for people with pedophilic thoughts.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He claims he left as soon as he realized the mistake, but the timestamps tell a different story -- from the photos, it looks like Jim was in the chat for almost an hour.
      
    
            We reached out to Jim's lawyer about his firing, and she had no comment.
